Femmes, Québécoises, voilées… et exclues: Women, Quebecers, Veiled… and Excluded – They Respond in the Streets
Des femmes voilées témoignent à Montréal: Veiled women speak out in Montréal on Nov. 29, 2025: Bill 94 shuts them out of public-sector jobs, and they fear being rendered invisible.
Manifestante contre la loi 94 tenant une: A protester against Bill 94 holds a sign and speaks to passersby and the media. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
Cet article est né d’une question simple: This article began with a simple question: what are women who wear the hijab actually going through as a new law further restricts their access to work?
Pour y répondre, j’ai passé l’après-midi: To find out, I spent the afternoon of November 29 in the middle of the “Dans la rue pour le Québec” march, following several women (students, early childhood educators, aspiring teachers, mothers) who had come to march against Bill 94. I hadn’t planned to focus on them at the start, but their stories, their worry and their determination quickly took over.
Mon objectif, en tant que journaliste, n: My aim as a journalist wasn’t to speak for them, but to document what they are living through: employment doors closing; the difficult, even impossible, choice being imposed on them; the fear of becoming invisible in public space. The accounts reported here were gathered during the march or just before it, amid the din of slogans and the movements of the procession.
<strong>Elles s’appellent Houda, Marwa,: Their names are Houda, Marwa, Saliha and Zoubida. They are Quebecers, and they are teachers or in training. They have something else in common: they wear the hijab. Since Bill 94 was adopted, their access to the job market has been shrinking. On Saturday, November 29, they joined thousands of demonstrators in downtown Montréal to say no to this law and to a series of measures seen as an attack on freedoms.
Il est un peu plus de 13 h 30 lorsque la: It’s just after 1:30 p.m. when the “<l1>Dans la rue pour le Québec</l1>” march sets off from Place du Canada. Under a November sun, blue-collar and white-collar workers advance shoulder to shoulder along René-Lévesque Boulevard. Teachers, parents and citizens mingle; all have come at the call of the unions to denounce the CAQ government’s “authoritarian drift.”
Certains poussent des poussettes, d’autr: Some push strollers, others hold flags or homemade signs. Side by side, the women we followed make their way through the crowd, each wearing her hijab with the same quiet assurance. Despite their different paths, they share one concern: after having been excluded from schools, they say, Bill 94 – a Quebec law aimed at strengthening secularism in the education system, adopted on October 30, 2025 – threatens their right to work in daycares and, more broadly, their place in society.
<strong>Houda Djilani : refuser l’invisi: Houda Djilani: refusing to be made invisible
Bien avant que la marche ne démarre, Hou: Well before the march starts, Houda Djilani is already standing at the top of the steps of Mary, Queen of the World Cathedral, sign raised, as if to say: “I’m here, I refuse to be erased!” This almost strategic position seems to respond directly to the feeling of being made invisible that many women who wear the headscarf say they experience in the face of recently adopted laws.
Âgée de 34 ans, Houda est diplômée en pr: Houda, 34, holds a degree in pharmaceutical production. But she turned toward education, a choice that owes nothing to chance or to the political climate. “I’ve always been drawn to education. A teacher’s role is a bit like a mother’s,” she explains. She also talks about the influence of her father, himself a teacher: “He always encouraged me to become a teacher.” Today, she is finishing a bachelor’s degree in preschool education and works as a substitute in schools, often as a supervisor. “I love being in schools,” she says quietly.
Mais la loi 94 vient bousculer ses plans: But Bill 94 is upending her plans. Like many women who want to practise this profession, she sees her professional future suddenly closing. “School boards have started calling colleagues to ask them to choose between their hijab and their job,” she says. And yet, she says, at university, “the guidance counsellors assured me and my veiled classmates that the secularism laws wouldn’t affect us.”
Aujourd’hui, à quelques mois du diplôme,: Today, a few months before graduating, she no longer knows what to say when asked what she’ll do afterward. “I have no idea,” she admits.
Pour elle, de toute façon, le choix prop: For her, in any case, the choice employers are offering isn’t a choice at all: “They [teachers who wear the hijab] are not going to take off their hijab, they are not going to give up their identity.”
Quand Houda parle de ses collègues, ses: When Houda talks about her colleagues, her hands come alive. She describes them as “courageous and competent,” women who are “judged because of the hijab” before their work is even assessed. Her own path ties her to them: after years of study and changing direction, she simply wants to “contribute, like everyone else.”
Foule de manifestants contre la loi 94,: A crowd of demonstrators against Bill 94, November 29, 2025. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
Dans la foule, elle respire un Québec to: In the crowd, she senses a tolerant, caring Quebec, a world away from the “disappointing” and “discouraging” one she laments hearing in some political speeches and on social media.
L’apprentie enseignante, qui réside à Sa: The aspiring teacher, who lives in Saint-Léonard, echoes the dozens, even hundreds, of women who, like her, chose to march to protect their rights and their children’s future: “We hope there will be change, whether it’s for workers’ rights, whether it’s… We’re here for our own good and for everyone’s good.”
<strong>Marwa* : « Ai-je encore ma place: Marwa*: “Do I still have a place in Quebec?”
Plus loin dans la foule, Marwa<em>* </em: Farther along in the crowd, Marwa* walks pushing a double stroller, accompanied by her husband, who was born in Sherbrooke and works as an engineer in the public sector, and their two young children. She prefers not to give her real name, but wants to tell her story. Having arrived in Quebec at the age of six, Marwa has lived her whole life here. Yet, she confides, “today, I’m asking myself a question I’ve never asked before: ‘Do I have a place in Quebec?’”
Ce sentiment, raconte la jeune maman, s’: This feeling, the young mother says, took hold when the CAQ came to power. “We’ve never seen as much racism as we see under the Legault government.” Marwa dreams of becoming a psychologist, and she doesn’t have far to go to earn her degree. But today, she sees her professional future narrowing: “If I want to work in the public system, I’ll be restricted. In education, it’s already impossible. I couldn’t be a school psychologist either.” And yet, “it’s not my hijab I explain to my clients, it’s my expertise,” she says indignantly.
Autour d’elle, d’autres femmes vivent le: Around her, other women share the same worries, like her sister, an education student who is now unable to do her internships while wearing her hijab; or her children’s early childhood educator, who is spared by the grandfather clause but whose career advancement is now conditional on her hijab. “What does that mean? That women who wear the hijab can’t advance. So we’re going backward on women’s rights!”
Pour les femmes portant le voile, le cha: For women who wear the hijab, the field of possibilities has been shrinking for several years: first, teaching at every level of the public system was closed to them by Bill 21 in 2019; now, child care services are being taken away by Bill 94. Zoubida’s path, forced to change careers twice, shows how gradually the trap has closed.
Après avoir réussi ses tests et obtenu s: After passing her tests and obtaining her teaching licence, Zoubida Gasmi, 44, had to abandon her career plans when Bill 21 came into force. “Seeing that I couldn’t teach because of Bill 21, I started training in early childhood education,” she says. But the new Bill 94 now thwarts her plans and postpones her return to work sine die.
Sur la rue Sainte-Catherine, Zoubida mar: On Sainte-Catherine Street, Zoubida walks with a firm step. Her face shows a mix of dismay, anger and indignation at what she describes as a repeated injustice. For her, it isn’t only a question of employment, but also of dignity: “My hijab is my right. Nobody can force me to take it off. Quebec, Canada, is a country of freedom. And I want to exercise that freedom.”
En marchant parmi les familles, Zoubida: Walking among the families, Zoubida watches the children studying the signs and slogans. Her own son sometimes asks her why she doesn’t teach. “He sees the injustice, he understands,” she says. The succession of laws thus doesn’t affect only adults: it also shapes how the youngest see their role models.
<strong>Saliha : marcher pour celles qui: Saliha: marching for those who will be affected tomorrow
Plus loin dans la manifestation, Saliha: Farther along in the demonstration, Saliha walks at an unhurried, almost composed pace. Among the group of veiled women around her, she is something of an elder. Some look to her as one seeks approval. She smiles gently: “I’m here a bit like the dean, I think,” she says.
Employée d’expérience dans une école de: An experienced employee at a school in Montréal-Nord, Saliha benefits from the grandfather clause. She knows she won’t lose her job, but she isn’t worried about herself. “Around me, no one is affected for now, but I’m out here for others, for our children, for our daughters,” she says, watching the crowd where strollers and teenagers chanting slogans file past.
Elle parle d’une pente glissante qu’elle: She speaks of a slippery slope she sees taking shape: “If we let it happen now, it’ll end up like France. Over there, they even ban the hijab for students at school and university.” There is no anger in her voice, but a lucid weariness, that of someone who has watched things deteriorate over the years.
Saliha évoque aussi ce qu’elle considère: Saliha also points to what she considers a double standard. “If you want secularism, you have to apply it everywhere,” she says, referring to the Christmas trees that are everywhere in schools and public services.
Si elle marche aujourd’hui, c’est pour m: If she is marching today, it is to keep open a horizon that she sees darkening for the youngest. “We can’t let it close on them,” she whispers. Her presence that day has something of a protective gesture about it – that of a woman moving forward for those who will have to carry on after her.
<strong>Hadjira : retirer le voile pour: Hadjira: taking off the hijab to work is not an option
La veille de la marche du 29 novembre, H: The day before the November 29 march, Hadjira Belkacem tells her story in front of La Converse’s camera. She adjusts her hijab, takes a long breath, then begins. Her tone is calm, but every sentence seems charged with a tension that has built up over the years.
La militante communautaire, connue notam: The community activist, known in particular for her involvement in the Muslim cemeteries issue, is an educator by trade who ran her own home daycare for 14 years. After a forced break that was prolonged by illness, Hadjira planned to return to work. And then Bill 94 came down. “I’m questioning myself. Will I go back into the workforce without my headscarf? That’s impossible. I’ve worn my headscarf since I was 11, I grew up with it,” she says firmly. The woman in her fifties, who arrived in Quebec in 2006, speaks of her way of dressing as a part of herself. And what hurts her most is that “a politician would come and tell me how to dress”!
À mesure qu’elle parle, sa colère affleu: As she speaks, her anger surfaces. Hadjira Belkacem thinks of her single-parent colleagues who risk losing their jobs: “At least I have my husband, I have my children. But others have no one.” She describes a daily life made heavier by eroding purchasing power, on top of which successive laws have piled: “Life here is hard. Adding even more weight on our shoulders is unjust and inhumane.” For her, the scope of this law goes beyond the job market and reflects a broader logic of the CAQ government – “a minority that wants to erase Muslim women from public space.”

Au fil de la marche, les manifestants se: As the march goes on, the demonstrators mingle. Conversations strike up spontaneously. Strangers congratulate one another on the diversity represented in the procession. The signs are reflected in the windows of buildings, and the crowd moves forward amid a mix of chants and slogans.
À la fin, et malgré la fatigue, les mani: At the end, despite the fatigue, the demonstrators leave the square with a palpable energy. For Houda, Marwa, Saliha and Zoubida, the November 29 demonstration was not only a political gesture: it was also a way of claiming their place in a Quebec where access to employment, dignity and freedom of conscience should not be conditional on their appearance.
Leur message est clair : le Québec doit: Their message is clear: Quebec must be a place of freedom and respect for everyone, regardless of their origins or religion.
Voile, emploi et loi 94 : témoignages de: Hijab, employment and Bill 94: accounts from women excluded, shared during the November 29, 2025 march
À Montréal le 29 novembre, des femmes vo: In Montréal on November 29, veiled women — students, early childhood educators, mothers — marched against Bill 94, describing how the law restricts their access to jobs in education and child care services. Their stories reveal fear, indignation and a sense of being made invisible: broken career paths, a compromised professional future, and the fight for dignity in public space.
